what_it_means_paragraphs: Light fixture installation covers everything from replacing a builder-grade flush-mount with a pendant you picked out online, to mounting a heavy chandelier in a two-story foyer, to adding recessed lighting where none existed before. Every fixture connects to your home's electrical system through a junction box — and that junction box has to be rated for the fixture's weight, wired correctly, and grounded to code. A loose connection behind drywall is invisible until it overheats — if you notice flickering or warm switch plates, that warrants electrical troubleshooting in {city_name} before installing anything new. That's why {license_state} requires a licensed electrician for new fixture wiring and circuit work.

Chandelier installation is the job most homeowners underestimate. A 75-pound chandelier needs a fan-rated or heavy-duty junction box bolted to ceiling joists — not just the drywall. The dimmer has to be compatible with the fixture's bulb type (LED chandeliers are especially sensitive to dimmer mismatch, causing flicker or buzz). If the dimmer or switch needs replacing as part of the install, our outlet and switch installation in {city_name} service covers that in the same visit. Recessed lighting layouts require IC-rated housings where insulation touches the can, and proper spacing so the room lights evenly. If you bought a fixture at a showroom, Home Depot, or Wayfair, we install it — any brand, any style.

problem_cards.title: Chandelier installation in a two-story foyer
problem_cards.body: Heavy chandeliers (50-200+ lbs) in two-story foyers require structural support rated for the fixture weight, proper junction box reinforcement, and safe access at height. We assess the ceiling structure, install a rated fan brace or mounting bracket, and wire the fixture to code. This is a two-person job — don't attempt it with a YouTube video and a ladder.

problem_cards.title: Replacing an old fixture with a modern one
problem_cards.body: Swapping a flush-mount for a pendant, or a builder-grade fixture for something you actually chose, is the most common call we get. The wiring is usually in place but the junction box, dimmer switch, or mounting bracket may need updating. We handle the full swap — old fixture down, new fixture up, tested and working.

problem_cards.title: Installing a light where there wasn't one before
problem_cards.body: Adding a new ceiling light means running wire from the nearest circuit, cutting a ceiling hole, installing a junction box, and connecting the fixture. If there's attic access, it's straightforward. If the ceiling is finished with no access above, we run conduit or fish wire through the wall cavity. Either way, it's permitted work. While we're running new circuits, many {city_name} homeowners also add hardwired smoke alarms since the wiring access is already open.

problem_cards.title: Recessed lighting installation
problem_cards.body: Recessed (can) lights require cutting holes in the ceiling, ensuring insulation clearance (IC-rated housings), running wire between each fixture, and connecting to a dimmer. We install 4, 6, 8, or more in a layout that actually lights the room evenly — not the builder-grade placement that leaves dark corners.

problem_cards.title: Outdoor lighting installation
problem_cards.body: Exterior wall sconces, soffit lights, pathway bollards, and landscape lighting all require weatherproof junction boxes, GFCI protection, and outdoor-rated wiring. Outdoor outlets feeding landscape lighting need the same weatherproof treatment we cover under outdoor outlet installation in {city_name}. We install exterior fixtures to code so they survive Northern Virginia weather and don't trip your indoor circuits.

problem_cards.title: Ceiling fan to light fixture swap (or vice versa)
problem_cards.body: Ceiling fans and light fixtures use the same junction box location but different mounting hardware and wiring (fans need a fan-rated box for the vibration and weight). Swapping one for the other means verifying or upgrading the box, rewiring the switch (fan has two circuits — light and motor), and mounting the new unit.

problem_cards.title: Customer-supplied fixture — you bought it, we install it
problem_cards.body: You picked the perfect fixture online or at a showroom. We install it. We work with any brand, any style, any weight — just make sure it arrives with mounting hardware and instructions. If parts are missing, we'll tell you before we start.

process_section_title: Our installation process — what happens when you call

process_steps.title: Tell us about the fixture and the location
process_steps.body: We ask what fixture you're installing (or whether you need help choosing), where it's going (room, ceiling type, height), and whether there's existing wiring at the location. For chandeliers, we ask about weight and whether the ceiling is drywall-only or has structural backing.

process_steps.title: On-site assessment if needed
process_steps.body: For straightforward replacements, we can quote over the phone. For new locations, heavy chandeliers, or recessed lighting layouts, we visit the house, look at the ceiling, check the circuit, and give a written estimate. No charge for the visit in our primary service area.

process_steps.title: Installation — typically 1-3 hours per fixture
process_steps.body: We arrive with the tools and hardware. Simple replacements take 30-60 minutes. Chandeliers and new-location installs take 2-3 hours. Recessed lighting layouts (6-8 fixtures) take half a day. We test every fixture and clean up when we're done.

process_steps.title: Dimmer and switch upgrades included
process_steps.body: If your new fixture needs a dimmer switch, or if the existing switch doesn't match (toggle vs. rocker, single-pole vs. three-way), we swap it as part of the install. No separate appointment needed. If you also need EV charger installation in {city_name} or other panel work while we're at the house, we can bundle the projects.

faq_items.question: Can I install a chandelier myself?
faq_items.answer_html: A small, lightweight chandelier (under 35 lbs) on an existing junction box is technically a DIY swap if you're comfortable turning off the breaker, testing with a voltage tester, and matching wires. But most chandeliers worth calling 'chandeliers' weigh 50-200+ lbs and require a fan-rated or heavy-duty junction box secured to ceiling joists — not just drywall anchors. Two-story foyer installations add height risk and typically need two people plus scaffolding. If the fixture is heavy, the ceiling is high, or you're uncertain about the box rating, hire a licensed electrician. The cost of doing it right is far less than repairing a fallen fixture.

faq_items.question: How long does it take to install a light fixture?
faq_items.answer_html: A simple fixture swap — removing the old unit and connecting a new one to existing wiring with a standard junction box — takes 30-60 minutes per fixture. Chandelier installations and new-location installs (where we run wire, install a junction box, and add a switch) take 2-3 hours. Recessed lighting layouts with 6-8 fixtures plus a dimmer take half a day. If you're scheduling multiple fixtures in one visit, we can usually knock out 3-5 simple swaps in a single morning. We confirm the time estimate before we arrive so you know what to expect.

faq_items.question: Can you install a light where there isn't one now?
faq_items.answer_html: Yes. Adding a new ceiling light where none existed means running wire from the nearest circuit to the new location, cutting a hole in the ceiling, installing a junction box, and connecting the fixture. If there's attic access above the ceiling, the job is straightforward — we run Romex through the attic and drop it to the new box. If the ceiling is finished with no access above (common in {city_name}'s two-story colonials), we fish wire through wall cavities or run surface conduit. Either way, it's permitted work in {county} and typically requires an electrical permit filed through the PLUS system.

faq_items.question: What's the difference between a regular junction box and a fan-rated box?
faq_items.answer_html: A standard junction box is rated for roughly 35-50 lbs of static weight — enough for a typical flush-mount or small pendant. A fan-rated box (sometimes called a 'fan brace box') is engineered to handle both heavier weight (up to 70+ lbs, depending on the model) and the continuous vibration that ceiling fans produce. NEC code requires a fan-rated box for ceiling fans and any fixture heavy enough to exceed the standard box's rating. For large chandeliers that exceed even fan-rated limits, we install a heavy-duty mounting bracket bolted directly to ceiling joists. We check the box before every installation — if it needs upgrading, we replace it as part of the job.

faq_items.question: Do you install recessed lighting?
faq_items.answer_html: Yes. Recessed (can) lighting is one of the most popular upgrade requests we get from {city_name} homeowners — especially in kitchens, living rooms, and finished basements. We use IC-rated housings (insulation-contact rated) so the cans can sit against attic insulation without creating a fire hazard. We lay out the fixture positions to light the room evenly — not the builder-grade pattern that clusters lights near walls and leaves the center dim. Every recessed layout includes a compatible dimmer switch. We price recessed lighting per layout (number of fixtures plus the dimmer) and give you a written estimate after measuring the room.
